title: Structs: Properties, Initializers and Methods
theory: A 'struct' is a value type that groups data (properties) and behavior (methods) under one name, such as 'struct Ponto { var x = 0; var y = 0 }'. Stored properties hold a value (with or without a default), while computed properties calculate their value on every access, like 'var area: Double { largura * altura }'. Every struct gets a free memberwise initializer, for example 'Ponto(x: 1, y: 2)', and you can write your own 'init'; if it is declared inside the struct body, the memberwise one is no longer generated (declare it in an 'extension' to keep both). Methods that change properties must be marked 'mutating', because a struct is a value type. 'static' members belong to the type ('Config.versao') rather than to each instance. Because structs have copy semantics, 'var b = a' creates an independent copy: changing 'b' does not affect 'a'. Also, an instance stored in a 'let' is completely immutable, even if its properties are 'var'. Nested types (an 'enum' inside a struct) help organize code. Apple's guidance is to prefer structs and use classes only when you need identity, inheritance or shared state. The certification covers properties, init, methods and creating instances.
corporateCase: A banking app models each 'Transacao' as a struct with amount, date and category. Since it is a value type, passing the transaction to another screen can never change it by accident, which makes testing easier and avoids shared-state bugs.
gameCase: A game defines 'struct Posicao' with x and y and a 'mutating mover(para:)' method. Saving the previous position is just copying the struct, which makes it easy to implement undo for moves.

quiz.question: Given 'struct Pessoa { var nome: String; var idade = 0 }', which call compiles using the memberwise initializer?
quiz.explanation: Properties with a default value (idade) become optional parameters, but 'nome' is required, needs its label, and arguments follow declaration order.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a stored and a computed property?
options: A computed property saves its value to disk automatically
A stored property can only be declared with let
There is no difference; they are just different syntaxes
A computed property stores nothing: it calculates its value on every access from other data
quiz.explanation: 'var area: Double { largura * altura }' takes no storage of its own; it is recalculated each time it is read. A stored property keeps a value in the instance.

quiz.question: What happens with 'let p = Ponto(x: 1, y: 2); p.x = 5'?
options: Compile error: a struct instance in a let is fully immutable
It works, since x is declared with var
It works, but only inside mutating methods
It compiles with a warning and ignores the assignment
quiz.explanation: Since a struct is a value type, declaring the instance with 'let' makes all its properties immutable, even 'var' ones. With a class it would differ, because the reference is what is constant.

quiz.question: What is the output? 'var a = Ponto(x: 1); var b = a; b.x = 9; print(a.x, b.x)'
quiz.explanation: Structs have copy semantics: 'var b = a' creates an independent copy. Changing b.x does not change a.x.

quiz.question: Why do methods that change a struct's properties need 'mutating'?
options: So the method can be overridden in subclasses
Because 'self' is immutable by default in value types; 'mutating' allows changing the instance itself
To prevent the method from being called outside the file
quiz.explanation: In structs and enums, methods do not change self by default. 'mutating' states the intent and can only be called on instances declared with 'var'.

quiz.question: How do you access 'static let versao' declared in 'struct Config'?
quiz.explanation: Static members belong to the type, so they are accessed with the type name, without creating an instance.

quiz.question: What happens when you declare a custom 'init' inside the struct body?
options: The automatic memberwise initializer is no longer generated
quiz.explanation: To keep both, declare the custom init in an 'extension' of the struct. Inside the body, only your init exists.

quiz.question: According to Apple's guidance, when should you choose a class over a struct?
options: Whenever the type has more than three properties
When you want the type to be faster in every case
When you need shared identity, inheritance or Objective-C interoperability
quiz.explanation: Apple recommends starting with a struct. A class is for when the instance must be shared by reference, inherit from another class or use NSObject-based APIs.

extraQuiz.question: Given 'struct Circulo { var raio = 1.0; var diametro: Double { raio * 2 } }', what happens with 'c.diametro = 10'?
options: Compile error: the computed property only has a getter
It works only if c is let
extraQuiz.explanation: Without a 'set', the property is read-only. To accept assignment you would need to declare both get and set.

extraQuiz.question: What happens in 'func f(_ p: Ponto) { p.x = 1 }', where Ponto is a struct?
options: Error: parameters are constants; you would need 'inout' and 'var' at the call site
It changes the caller's original point
It creates a copy and changes it, without error
It works if the call passes the point as a 'var'
extraQuiz.explanation: Parameters are constants inside the function. To change the caller's variable you use 'inout' (passing '&ponto'). With a class you could change properties, since p is a reference.

extraQuiz.question: How do you refer to the enum 'Status' declared inside 'struct Pedido'?
extraQuiz.explanation: Nested types live in the scope of the outer type and are accessed with a dot, like Pedido.Status.pago.

extraQuiz.question: Given 'var lista = [Ponto(x: 1)]; var copia = lista; copia[0].x = 5', what is the value of 'lista[0].x'?
extraQuiz.explanation: Arrays and structs are value types: 'copia' is independent of 'lista', and the change does not propagate.

extraQuiz.question: In 'init(x: Int) { self.x = x }', why is 'self' needed?
options: To tell the property apart from the parameter with the same name
So the struct becomes a class
extraQuiz.explanation: Inside the init, a bare 'x' refers to the parameter (shadowing). 'self.x' points to the instance's property.

extraQuiz.question: Which type is the best choice to model a coordinate with latitude and longitude?
options: class, so it can be shared
struct, since it is small value data with no need for identity
extraQuiz.explanation: Coordinates are simple values: two equal coordinates are interchangeable. This is the typical case for a struct (that is how MapKit treats CLLocationCoordinate2D).

title: Classes, Inheritance and Access Control
theory: A 'class' is a reference type: several variables can point to the same instance, and '===' checks whether two references are the same object (identity), unlike '==' which compares values. Every designated initializer of a class must initialize its own properties and only then call 'super.init'; 'convenience' initializers delegate to a designated one of the same class with 'self.init'. 'required init' forces subclasses to implement it. A subclass inherits from a superclass and redefines behavior with 'override', calling 'super' when it wants to reuse the original; 'final' prevents inheritance or overriding. 'deinit' runs when the instance is released by ARC (reference count zero). Access control has five levels: 'open' (other modules can use and subclass), 'public' (use, but not subclass), 'internal' (the default, inside the module), 'fileprivate' (inside the file) and 'private' (inside the declaration); 'private(set)' allows reading from outside but writing only from inside. Enums are types of their own too: 'enum' with raw values ('enum Dia: Int'), associated values ('case erro(String)'), exhaustive 'switch' and 'CaseIterable' to get 'allCases'. Rule of thumb: enum for a closed set of states, struct for data, class for identity and inheritance.
corporateCase: A corporate app has a base class 'Documento' with subclasses 'Contrato' and 'Fatura' that override 'validar()'. The 'protocolo' property is 'private(set)', so screens can read the number but only the model itself changes it.
gameCase: In a game, 'class Inimigo' has subclasses such as 'Chefe', which overrides 'atacar()'. Several parts of the game hold a reference to the same enemy, and the level state is an enum with cases like menu, jogando and fimDeJogo.

quiz.question: Given 'class Caixa { var v = 0 }', 'let a = Caixa(); let b = a; b.v = 5; print(a.v)' prints:
quiz.explanation: Classes are reference types: a and b point to the same object. 'let' fixes the reference but does not prevent changing 'var' properties.

quiz.question: In a subclass designated init, what is the correct order?
options: Initialize the subclass's own properties and then call super.init
Call super.init and then initialize own properties
quiz.explanation: In Swift's two-phase initialization, the subclass must initialize all its properties before delegating to the superclass init.

quiz.question: Which keyword is required to redefine an inherited method?
quiz.explanation: The compiler requires 'override' to make explicit that you are replacing the inherited method, avoiding accidental overrides.

quiz.question: What does 'final class Servico' guarantee?
options: Nobody can create subclasses of Servico
Servico only lives in the current file
quiz.explanation: 'final' prevents inheritance and overriding, which also lets the compiler optimize calls.

quiz.question: Which access level allows ANOTHER module to subclass the class and override its methods?
quiz.explanation: 'public' allows use from outside but not subclassing or overriding; 'open' allows both. It is the typical level for framework classes such as UIViewController.

quiz.question: What does 'private(set) var total = 0' do?
options: Any code can read total, but only internal code writes it
quiz.explanation: 'private(set)' restricts only the setter. It exposes the value for reading and protects the update rule inside the type.

quiz.question: When does a class's 'deinit' run?
options: When the last strong reference to the instance goes away and ARC releases it
quiz.explanation: deinit is called automatically before memory is released and exists only in classes. Strong reference cycles prevent it from running.

quiz.question: Given 'enum Direcao: CaseIterable { case norte, sul, leste, oeste }', what is the value of 'Direcao.allCases.count'?
quiz.explanation: CaseIterable generates the 'allCases' collection with every case, useful to fill menus and Pickers.

extraQuiz.question: Given 'enum Planeta: Int { case mercurio = 1, venus, terra }', what is the value of 'Planeta.terra.rawValue'?
extraQuiz.explanation: With an integer raw value, the following cases increment automatically: mercurio = 1, venus = 2, terra = 3.

extraQuiz.question: What is the difference between a raw value and an associated value in enums?
options: They are the same feature with different names
Raw values allow different types per case
A raw value is fixed and the same for every case of that type; an associated value stores different data each time the case is used
extraQuiz.explanation: 'case erro(String)' stores a different text on each use, extracted in the 'switch' with 'case .erro(let msg)'. A raw value is a constant defined in the declaration.

extraQuiz.question: What is the difference between '==' and '===' on classes?
options: '==' compares values (if Equatable); '===' checks whether they are the same instance
extraQuiz.explanation: Two different instances can hold equal data ('==' true) and still be distinct objects ('===' false).

extraQuiz.question: A 'convenience init' must:
options: Call, directly or indirectly, a designated init of its own class with self.init
extraQuiz.explanation: Convenience inits delegate 'across' (same class); only designated inits delegate 'up' (super.init).

extraQuiz.question: What is the difference between 'private' and 'fileprivate'?
options: private applies to the whole module
private limits to the declaration (and extensions in the same file); fileprivate opens up the whole file
extraQuiz.explanation: The default, with no modifier, is 'internal' (the whole module). Preferring the most restrictive level possible helps encapsulation.

extraQuiz.question: Which type best represents the states 'loading', 'error' and 'success' of a screen?
options: enum, since it is a closed set of cases, with associated data if needed
extraQuiz.explanation: An enum with an exhaustive 'switch' makes the compiler warn when a state is forgotten, and associated values carry each state's data.

title: Advanced Properties and Property Wrappers
theory: Beyond simple stored properties, Swift offers features that control how a value is initialized, read and written. A 'lazy var' property only computes its initial value the first time it is accessed, which is useful for expensive work; it must be 'var'. Computed properties use 'get' and 'set' (with an implicit 'newValue') and store no value. Observers 'willSet' (receives 'newValue') and 'didSet' (receives 'oldValue') run when the value changes, but not during the type's own initialization. 'static' properties (and 'class' ones, in classes, which can be overridden) belong to the type. Key paths such as '\Pessoa.nome' reference a property without reading it, and are used with 'pessoa[keyPath: \.nome]', 'map' and in SwiftUI and SwiftData. A property wrapper is a type marked with '@propertyWrapper' that has 'wrappedValue' (the real value) and optionally 'projectedValue', accessed with '$'. SwiftUI is built this way: '@State' stores state and '$nome' hands out a 'Binding'; '@AppStorage' persists to UserDefaults and updates the view. Properties can also be Optional ('var apelido: String?'), with a default of nil, and read with optional chaining.
corporateCase: In a settings app, '@AppStorage("tema")' stores the chosen theme and the screen updates itself. A custom '@Limitado' wrapper guarantees the volume stays between 0 and 100 anywhere in the app.
gameCase: A game uses 'didSet' on 'vidas' to play a sound and show 'Game Over' when it reaches zero. The level map is a 'lazy' property, loaded only when the player enters the stage.

quiz.question: Why must a 'lazy' property be declared with 'var'?
options: Because lazy only works in classes
Because lazy turns the type into Optional
Because its initial value is only set later, on first access, which mutates the property
quiz.explanation: Since the instance is created without the value and it gets filled in later, the property cannot be a constant.

quiz.question: What is the difference between willSet and didSet?
options: willSet runs before the change (newValue); didSet runs after (oldValue)
quiz.explanation: Inside willSet the new value is in 'newValue'; in didSet the old value is in 'oldValue' and the property already holds the new one.

quiz.question: Given 'struct Vida { var valor: Int { didSet { print("mudou") } }; init() { valor = 3 } }', 'Vida()' prints:
options: Nothing, since observers do not run when assigning inside the type's own init
quiz.explanation: Observers only fire for changes after initialization. Assignments in the type's init set the initial value.

quiz.question: What characterizes a computed property?
options: It stores no value: it uses get (and optionally set) to calculate
quiz.explanation: It exposes a value derived from other properties; without set it is read-only.

quiz.question: What is the type of '\Pessoa.nome' when 'nome' is a 'let' of type String?
options: KeyPath<Pessoa, String>, which references the property and is used with [keyPath:]
quiz.explanation: Key paths represent the path to a property without reading its value; 'pessoa[keyPath: \.nome]' actually reads it.

quiz.question: In '@State var contador = 0', what do 'contador' and '$contador' represent?
options: contador is the wrappedValue (Int); $contador is the projectedValue (Binding<Int>)
quiz.explanation: Property wrappers expose the real value and, optionally, a projected value accessed with '$'. In @State it is a Binding to pass to child views.

quiz.question: How does SwiftUI use property wrappers such as @State?
options: It is a reserved compiler word with no Swift implementation
It copies the whole view on each change
@State is a type marked @propertyWrapper that stores the value outside the view struct and notifies SwiftUI when it changes
quiz.explanation: The wrapper keeps storage managed by SwiftUI and, when the value changes, invalidates the 'body'. It is a language feature, not compiler magic.

quiz.question: Which wrapper stores a simple preference in UserDefaults and updates the view on change?
quiz.explanation: @AppStorage reads and writes UserDefaults by key and rebuilds the view when the value changes. @State only keeps it in memory.

extraQuiz.question: What characterizes a 'static' property?
options: It is single and shared, belongs to the type, and is accessed as Type.property
There is one copy per instance
It can only be read inside init
extraQuiz.explanation: Use it for constants and settings of the type, such as 'Jogo.pontosMaximos'.

extraQuiz.question: Given the wrapper 'Limitado' with 'init(wrappedValue: Int) { v = min(wrappedValue, 10) }' and a setter with 'v = min(newValue, 10)', what does 'var j = Jogo(); j.vidas = 15; print(j.vidas)' print if 'struct Jogo { @Limitado var vidas = 3 }'?
extraQuiz.explanation: The wrappedValue setter caps the value at 10. The wrapper centralizes the rule and reuses it on any property.

extraQuiz.question: If 'var apelido: String?' in Pessoa, what is the type of 'pessoa.apelido?.count'?
extraQuiz.explanation: Optional chaining ends in nil when the property is nil and wraps the result in an Optional.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'class var' allow that 'static var' does not in a class?
options: Subclasses can override the computed type property
extraQuiz.explanation: static in a class is equivalent to 'final class': it cannot be overridden. A computed 'class var' can be redefined by subclasses.

extraQuiz.question: What is the correct argument for a child view that needs to read and write the parent's @State?
extraQuiz.explanation: Passing 'contador' sends only a copy. The '$' hands out a Binding, a read-write connection to the source of truth.

extraQuiz.question: What happens if, inside a property's didSet, you assign a new value to the property itself?
options: The observer is not called again for that assignment, so there is no infinite recursion
extraQuiz.explanation: Swift avoids recursion: assigning inside the property's own didSet changes the value without triggering the observers again.

title: Strings, Characters and Text
theory: In Swift, 'String' is a collection of 'Character', and each Character is a Unicode grapheme cluster: a single visible character, even if it uses several code points (for example '🇧🇷' counts as 1). That is why 'count' walks the text and there is no integer indexing: you use 'index(_:offsetBy:)' or 'startIndex'. Slicing a String (such as 'prefix(3)') returns a 'Substring', which shares memory with the original and must be converted with 'String(...)' to be stored. Interpolation '"Olá, \(nome)"' inserts values, and multiline literals use '"""'. Common methods: 'isEmpty', 'hasPrefix', 'hasSuffix', 'uppercased()', 'contains', 'split(separator:)', 'replacingOccurrences(of:with:)' and 'trimmingCharacters(in:)' (Foundation). Comparing with '==' is case-sensitive; for text shown to users use 'localizedCompare' and 'localizedCaseInsensitiveCompare'. For formatting, '.formatted()' applies language and region rules to numbers and dates, as in 'Date.now.formatted(date: .abbreviated, time: .omitted)'. Regular expressions use the 'Regex' type and literals like '/\d+/' (in Swift 5 language mode the bare-slash literal needs the bare-slash-regex option; the '#/\d+/#' form always works). 'AttributedString' stores per-range styles, and in SwiftUI a literal in 'Text("chave")' is a 'LocalizedStringKey' looked up in the translation files.
corporateCase: A sign-up app cleans what the user types with 'trimmingCharacters' and validates the tax ID format with a Regex. Dates and amounts in currency are displayed with '.formatted()', respecting the user's region.
gameCase: A game splits the typed command ('atacar goblin') with 'split(separator: " ")' to interpret verb and target. The interface texts use LocalizedStringKey to show the game in several languages.

quiz.question: What is '"🇧🇷".count' in Swift?
options: 1, since a Character is a grapheme cluster, even with several Unicode scalars
quiz.explanation: The flag is formed by two regional code points, but it appears as a single character. 'utf8.count' would return 8.

quiz.question: Why does 'let c = texto[1]' not compile?
options: Strings do not accept integer indices; you need String.Index, as in texto[texto.index(texto.startIndex, offsetBy: 1)]
quiz.explanation: Each Character can have a different size in memory, so integer access would cost O(n) and was left out on purpose.

quiz.question: What does 'let p = "Swift".prefix(3)' produce?
options: A Substring that shares storage with the original
quiz.explanation: To keep the result for a long time, convert it: 'String(p)'. That way the original String can be freed.

quiz.question: In a multiline literal with '"""', what defines the indentation removed?
options: The first character of the first line
The position of the closing '"""' delimiter
quiz.explanation: Any whitespace before the closing delimiter is stripped from every line, letting you indent the literal along with the code.

quiz.question: Which expression compares two Strings ignoring case?
quiz.explanation: '==' tells 'Ana' from 'ana'. For interface text, 'localizedCaseInsensitiveCompare' also respects language rules.

quiz.question: What does 'Date.now.formatted(date: .abbreviated, time: .omitted)' do?
options: Produces text with the date in abbreviated format, following the user's language and region
quiz.explanation: '.formatted()' uses the current Locale, so the same date appears as 'Oct 14, 2026' or '14 de out. de 2026' depending on region.

quiz.question: What does 'if "Pedido 42".contains(/\d+/)' do?
options: Returns true, since the Regex finds one or more digits
Returns false, since Foundation is missing
quiz.explanation: Regex literals '/.../' create a Regex value, which methods like contains and firstMatch(of:) accept in Swift 5.7 or later. In Swift 5 mode without the bare-slash-regex option, use '#/\d+/#'.

quiz.question: In SwiftUI, what is the difference between 'Text("bem_vindo")' and 'Text(verbatim: "bem_vindo")'?
options: The first treats the literal as a LocalizedStringKey and looks up the translation; the second shows the text as is
quiz.explanation: A literal in Text becomes a LocalizedStringKey. Use 'verbatim' when the text must not be translated, such as identifiers.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'let n = 3; print("\(n + 1) itens")' print?
extraQuiz.explanation: Interpolation '\( )' evaluates any Swift expression and inserts the result in the text.

extraQuiz.question: What is the result of '"a,,b".split(separator: ",").count'?
options: 2, since split drops empty parts by default
extraQuiz.explanation: The result is [Substring] with 'a' and 'b'. To keep the empty ones, use 'omittingEmptySubsequences: false'.

extraQuiz.question: Which declaration is invalid?
extraQuiz.explanation: A Character holds exactly one grapheme cluster. With two characters the compiler reports an error.

extraQuiz.question: Which type stores text with different styles per range (bold, links)?
extraQuiz.explanation: AttributedString associates attributes with ranges of text and can be displayed by Text in SwiftUI. It can also be created from Markdown.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'let s = "casa"; let t = s.replacingOccurrences(of: "a", with: "o"); print(s, t)' print?
extraQuiz.explanation: Strings are value types: replacingOccurrences returns a new String and does not change the original.

extraQuiz.question: Why use 'localizedCompare' instead of '<' to sort names shown to the user?
options: Because it applies the language's sorting rules, such as accents and case
Because '<' does not exist for String
extraQuiz.explanation: The '<' comparison uses Unicode order, which may put 'Ágata' after 'Zeca'. The localized one respects the user's Locale.
